newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Chechen police search for two British hostages.
newsitem.headline: Chechen police search for two British hostages.

text.p: Chechen police said on Sunday a special group had been set up to search for two British aid workers taken hostage in Russia's breakaway province.
Police gave no details of the search while both Russian and Chechen authorities expressed frustration over the failure of the two to report their presence in the volatile region.
British officials said on Saturday Camilla Carr and Jon James had been abducted from the house they were staying in on Wednesday night.
Half a dozen unknown people in masks came into the house brandishing guns and hauled them off to an unknown location, people living nearby told Reuters.

The pair had been working for a local little-known body called the Centre for Peacemaking and Community Development, helping children who suffered from a 21-month conflict between separatists and Russian troops which ended last August.
A spokesman for the British Embassy in Moscow, James Paver, said on Saturday checks were being made to try to locate them.
"Ministers have been informed and are deeply concerned," he said, adding that the non-governmental Centre had confirmed that two Britons had been working for it in Grozny since early April.

But Ivan Rybkin, secretary of Russia's powerful Security Council who plays an important role in peace talks with Chechnya, told Interfax news agency he did not know about the existence of the organisation.

"This whole story is rather surprising," Rybkin said, adding Russia had warned foreign states that their citizens should inform both the federal and local authorities about their presence in Chechnya. The pair had failed to do so, he said.
Chechen police said they had arrested three people on Saturday -- the pair's two bodyguards and an official from a Grozny organisation called the Centre for Child Rehabilitation.
No one at the Centre was immediately available for comment.

The abduction is the latest in a string of hostage-takings in the battle-scarred North Caucasus region, where tens of thousands of people died after Moscow sent in troops in late 1994 to try to stop it splitting from the rest of Russia.
The captors generally demand large sums of money, and securing the release of hostages, who are currently thought to number more than 20, is becoming increasingly difficult.
Major international aid organisations withdrew most of their staff from the region after six Red Cross workers were shot dead in their beds in December by unknown gunmen.
Some foreigners are still working in Grozny for smaller aid organisations, but they keep a low profile.

First vice-premier of Chechnya, Movladi Udugov, told Ekho Moskvy radio Chechen authorities often did not know about the presence of such organisations in the republic and would now work to collect data on them.
Paver said the embassy issued advice to travellers that Russia could not guarantee their safety in Chechnya but said there were other British aid workers there.

The last foreign captive in Chechnya, an Austrian businessman, was freed after an operation by the Chechen authorities at the end of May, Interfax said. Five Russian television journalists are among those still being held.

The separatist leaders of Chechnya, who successfully fought off Russian troops sent to crush their independence bid, have pledged to do all they can to free all the captives now being held, saying rogue groups of criminals are responsible.
Chechen President Aslan Maskhadov has issued a decree saying hostage-takers face the death penalty and their accomplices will get 15 years in jail.
